investor_pitch_game.title: Investor Pitch Arena
investor_pitch_game.description: Pitch any idea to a dynamic panel of AI investors. Face tough questions, handle objections, and win funding.

help_content.what_is: An investor pitch is your chance to convince people with money to back your idea. You'll face a panel of AI investors — each with their own personality and focus. They'll ask hard questions, raise objections, and decide whether to invest.
tips: Open with the problem, not the solution
Use specific numbers — investors love data
Know your market size (TAM, SAM, SOM)
Be honest about risks — investors respect transparency
Practice your 60-second elevator pitch until it's crisp
Have a clear 'ask' — how much money and for what

clarity_structure.description: Was the pitch clear, concise, and well-organized?

market_understanding.description: Does the pitcher understand the market, competition, and opportunity?

financial_viability.description: Are the numbers realistic? Is the revenue model sound?

confidence_delivery.description: Did they handle pressure? Speak with conviction?

objection_handling.description: How did they respond to tough questions and challenges?

investability.description: Would these investors actually put money in?

investor_pool.name: Kavita Sharma
investor_pool.focus: unit economics, margins, burn rate, CAC, LTV, runway
investor_pool.personality: Sharp and precise. Interrupts if numbers are vague. Respects founders who know their metrics cold. Will reject brilliant ideas with bad economics.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: What's your CAC and what's your 18-month runway at current burn?

investor_pool.name: Rohit Mehra
investor_pool.focus: scalability, technology moat, innovation, disruption potential
investor_pool.personality: Gets excited about big ideas but probes deep on technical feasibility. Loves founders who think 10x. Impatient with incremental improvements.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: What's your unfair advantage? Why can't Google build this in 6 months?

investor_pool.name: Anand Krishnan
investor_pool.focus: risk assessment, competitive threats, failure modes, market timing
investor_pool.personality: Challenges every assumption. Plays devil's advocate on purpose. Tests how founders handle pressure. Secretly invests in founders who don't crack.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: Three competitors failed at this exact thing. What makes you different?

investor_pool.name: Sunita Patel
investor_pool.focus: domain knowledge, regulatory landscape, industry partnerships, go-to-market
investor_pool.personality: Deep industry experience. Tests whether founders really understand the space or just read blog posts. Values first-hand customer discovery.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: Have you actually talked to 100 potential customers? What did they say?

investor_pool.name: Priya Nair
investor_pool.focus: user experience, customer pain points, retention, NPS, product-market fit
investor_pool.personality: Cares deeply about whether real users actually need this. Asks about user research, retention curves, and why people would switch from existing solutions.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: Show me one user who can't live without your product. What happens if you shut down?

investor_pool.name: Vikram Desai
investor_pool.focus: TAM, SAM, SOM, market trends, timing, competitive landscape
investor_pool.personality: Lives and breathes market data. Wants to know if the market is big enough and growing. Skeptical of 'everyone is our customer' claims.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: Your TAM slide says $50B. Walk me through how you get to your serviceable market.

investor_pool.name: Deepak Rao
investor_pool.focus: founding team, domain expertise, execution capability, founder-market fit
investor_pool.personality: Believes great teams beat great ideas. Asks about co-founder dynamics, past failures, and why THIS team is uniquely positioned. Warm but probing.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: Why are you the right person to build this? What's your unfair insight?

investor_pool.name: Meera Iyer
investor_pool.focus: social impact, sustainability, mission alignment, ESG metrics
investor_pool.personality: Invests for both returns and impact. Asks tough questions about measuring social outcomes. Excited by scalable solutions to real problems.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: How do you measure impact beyond revenue? What changes if you succeed?

investor_pool.name: Arjun Malhotra
investor_pool.focus: execution strategy, pivots, early traction, scrappiness, hustle
investor_pool.personality: Built and sold 3 companies. Speaks from experience. Tests whether founders are resourceful or just theoretical. Loves hustle stories.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: What have you done in the last 30 days without any funding?

investor_pool.name: Nisha Gupta
investor_pool.focus: non-obvious insights, unconventional approaches, market inefficiencies
investor_pool.personality: Always takes the opposite view. If everyone loves the idea, she'll find holes. If everyone hates it, she might invest. Tests conviction and independent thinking.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: Everyone agrees this is a good idea. That worries me. What does the crowd get wrong?

investor_pool.name: Ramesh Joshi
investor_pool.focus: 10-year vision, compounding advantages, moats, network effects
investor_pool.personality: Patient capital. Doesn't care about quick exits. Wants to know the 10-year vision. Asks about network effects, compounding advantages, and why this business gets stronger with time.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: Forget next quarter. What does this look like in 10 years?

investor_pool.name: Tanvi Shah
investor_pool.focus: growth channels, virality, distribution, user acquisition strategy
investor_pool.personality: Only cares about how you'll grow. Great product means nothing without distribution. Asks about growth loops, referral mechanics, and channel strategy.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: Product is nice. How do you get your first 10,000 users without spending money?

investor_pool.name: Karthik Venkatesh
investor_pool.focus: risk mitigation, failure scenarios, regulatory risk, key person risk
investor_pool.personality: Thinks about everything that can go wrong. Not pessimistic — just thorough. Respects founders who've thought about risks before being asked.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: What are the top 3 ways this company dies? What's your plan for each?

investor_pool.name: Lakshmi Sundaram
investor_pool.focus: founder growth, learning speed, coachability, strategic thinking
investor_pool.personality: Invests in people, not just ideas. Asks questions that teach, not just test. Watches how founders respond to feedback. Values coachability over confidence.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: If I told you your business model is wrong, what would you do?

investor_pool.name: Rajesh Kapoor
investor_pool.focus: valuation, deal terms, cap table, exit strategy, return multiples
investor_pool.personality: All business. Moves quickly to deal mechanics. Asks about valuation justification, dilution strategy, and exit scenarios. Respects founders who understand term sheets.
investor_pool.tough_question_style: You're asking for ₹1 crore at ₹5 crore valuation. Walk me through how you justify 20% of your company is worth this.

scenarios.title: EduLeap — AI Tutoring for Rural India
scenarios.description: You've built an AI-powered tutoring app that brings quality education to students in tier-3 cities and rural areas. It works offline, supports regional languages, and adapts to each student's learning pace.
scenarios.setting: A buzzing demo day at a Mumbai coworking space. Sunlight streams through large glass windows. Three investors sit across a wooden table, your laptop open with the EduLeap demo ready.
scenarios.pitch_topic: EduLeap — AI-powered offline tutoring for rural Indian students
coaching_tips: Lead with a specific student story — make the problem real
Explain how offline-first is your competitive moat
Show your pilot data from the 3 districts
Address the revenue model clearly — freemium needs volume
learning_objectives: Articulate a social impact business clearly

storybook_pages.title: The Problem You Saw
storybook_pages.text: Six months ago, you visited your grandmother's village in rural Maharashtra. You watched kids huddled around a single smartphone, trying to learn math from a YouTube video that kept buffering. That's when the idea hit you — what if AI could teach when the internet couldn't?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian village scene with children gathered around a single smartphone under a tree, struggling with poor internet, rural Maharashtra setting, warm sunset colors, emotional educational moment, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: EduLeap Is Born
storybook_pages.text: You built EduLeap — an app that downloads smart lessons and works completely offline. It speaks Marathi, Hindi, and Tamil. In your pilot across 3 districts, 5,000 students are already using it. Math scores went up 34%. Now you need funding to scale.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian student happily using a tablet app showing colorful math lessons, offline mode indicator visible, rural school background, diverse Indian students in the background, bright optimistic colors, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Demo Day
storybook_pages.text: The Mumbai coworking space is packed. You're the fourth pitch of the day. Three investors sit across the table — notebooks open, coffee cups half-empty. They've heard three pitches already. You have 8 minutes to convince them EduLeap is worth their money.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Modern Mumbai coworking space with three diverse Indian investors at a table, young founder standing with laptop presenting, demo day banner in background, professional yet startup casual atmosphere, illustration style

scenarios.title: TiffinBox — Hyperlocal Home Food Delivery
scenarios.description: You're building a platform connecting home cooks with office workers who miss ghar ka khana. No restaurants, no cloud kitchens — just real home-cooked meals from verified aunties and uncles in the neighborhood.
scenarios.setting: A startup accelerator's pitch night in Bangalore. The room is full of other founders and mentors. Your panel has three investors who've seen dozens of food delivery pitches.
scenarios.pitch_topic: TiffinBox — home-cooked meal marketplace connecting home cooks with nearby offices
coaching_tips: Acknowledge the competitive landscape (Swiggy, Zomato) upfront
Emphasize the 'home-cooked' moat — no one else does this
Show unit economics per order clearly
Address supply-side quality control proactively
learning_objectives: Present unit economics and growth metrics

storybook_pages.title: Missing Home Food
storybook_pages.text: It started when your roommate Sneha, working 12-hour shifts at an IT park, broke down crying over another bad biryani from a cloud kitchen. 'I just want food that tastes like home,' she said. You looked around the office — 500 people, all feeling the same way.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian office worker looking disappointed at takeaway food container, modern Bangalore IT park cafeteria setting, other workers in background also looking at mediocre food, relatable moment, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Aunty Network
storybook_pages.text: Three streets away, Lakshmi Aunty cooks the best dal chawal in Koramangala. She has time, she has skill, and she could use extra income. You connected her with 50 hungry techies. Word spread. Today, 200 home cooks serve 1,200 daily orders. TiffinBox was born.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Warm Indian home kitchen with a smiling middle-aged Indian woman cooking multiple tiffin boxes, neatly packed lunch boxes ready for delivery, cozy kitchen with spices and utensils, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Pitch Night
storybook_pages.text: Bangalore's startup accelerator is buzzing. The food is catered (ironically, from a cloud kitchen). Three investors who've seen every food delivery pitch in India are waiting. They know Swiggy's numbers by heart. Can you convince them that TiffinBox is different?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Bangalore startup accelerator event space at night, stage with spotlight, three investors at a panel table, young founder approaching the stage, other founders in audience, energetic atmosphere, illustration style

scenarios.title: TechFest — College Club Funding Pitch
scenarios.description: You're the president of your college's tech club. You need ₹2 lakh from the student council to organize TechFest — a three-day hackathon and tech conference. The council has a limited budget and 8 clubs competing for funds.
scenarios.setting: Your college's seminar hall. The student council president and two faculty advisors sit behind a desk. Other club presidents watch from the audience — this is competitive.
scenarios.pitch_topic: TechFest 2026 — A three-day college hackathon bringing industry speakers and 500+ students
coaching_tips: Show how TechFest benefits ALL students, not just the tech club
Present your sponsorship efforts — you've already raised ₹80K
Address past events — what went well and what you improved
Have a clear budget breakdown ready
learning_objectives: Pitch to a budget committee with competing priorities
Justify spending with concrete impact metrics
Handle questions about ROI for the institution

storybook_pages.title: The Annual Budget War
storybook_pages.text: It's that time of year again. Eight clubs, one student council, and a fixed budget. The drama club wants ₹1.5 lakh for their annual play. The sports club needs new equipment. And you — you need ₹2 lakh to pull off the biggest TechFest your college has ever seen.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian college seminar hall with multiple student club representatives waiting with their proposals, budget allocation meeting setting, college campus visible through windows, nervous energy, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Your Vision for TechFest
storybook_pages.text: Last year's TechFest had 200 students and one keynote speaker. This year, you've dreamed bigger — 500 students, 15 colleges, industry mentors from Infosys and Flipkart, and a 36-hour hackathon. You've already convinced 2 sponsors to put in ₹80K. But you need the council's backing.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Excited Indian college students at a tech hackathon, laptops open, coding together, colorful banners and tech company logos in background, energetic and creative atmosphere, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Your Turn to Present
storybook_pages.text: The drama club just finished their pitch. The council president looks tired. The faculty advisor is checking her watch. You're up next. You have 8 minutes to make them believe TechFest deserves the biggest share of the budget.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian college student standing up confidently from audience to approach a presentation podium, student council members at a desk looking expectant, seminar hall setting, moment of courage, illustration style

scenarios.title: JalShakti — Clean Water for 1000 Villages
scenarios.description: You've developed a low-cost solar-powered water purification system. It costs ₹15,000 per unit and can serve a village of 500 people. You need impact investment to manufacture and deploy 1,000 units across drought-prone districts.
scenarios.setting: An impact investment conference in Delhi. The panel includes investors who care about both returns and social outcomes. Your prototype sits on the table in front of you.
scenarios.pitch_topic: JalShakti — affordable solar-powered water purification for rural villages

predefined_metrics.ask: ₹2 crore impact investment for 1,000 units + distribution

coaching_tips: Lead with the human cost of dirty water — make it visceral
Show your pilot results from 23 villages with real health data
Address the revenue model — who pays? Government, NGOs, or communities?
Be clear about impact metrics beyond just units deployed
learning_objectives: Balance social mission with financial sustainability
Present impact metrics alongside business metrics
Handle questions about scalability of social ventures

storybook_pages.title: The Water Crisis
storybook_pages.text: In Bundelkhand, women walk 3 km every morning to fetch water. The water is brown. Children get sick. Hospitals are far. Last monsoon, your engineering college sent a team to study the problem. You came back with a prototype that could change everything.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian rural women carrying water pots on a dusty path in Bundelkhand region, dry landscape, brown water source visible in background, harsh sun, poignant and emotional scene, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Solar Solution
storybook_pages.text: Your JalShakti unit runs on solar power, costs ₹15,000 to build, and purifies 500 liters daily — enough for an entire village. In your pilot across 23 villages, waterborne diseases dropped 67%. The village panch loves it. Now you need to build 1,000 more.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Solar-powered water purification unit installed in an Indian village, villagers filling clean water in containers, solar panels gleaming, green trees in background, hope and technology meeting rural India, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Impact Investor Conference
storybook_pages.text: The Delhi conference hall smells like fresh carpet and ambition. Impact investors from across India have gathered. Your prototype sits on the table — small, solar-powered, and life-changing. Three investors lean forward. They want returns AND results. Can you deliver both?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Modern Delhi conference hall with impact investment banners, three investors examining a small solar water purifier prototype on the table, young Indian founder presenting passionately, professional setting, illustration style

scenarios.title: KrishiSense — Smart Agriculture Sensors
scenarios.description: You've built an IoT sensor kit that helps small farmers optimize irrigation, detect crop diseases early, and predict harvest timing. Each kit costs ₹3,000 and connects to a simple app that works in Hindi.
scenarios.setting: The final round of a national startup competition in Hyderabad. Prize: ₹50 lakh in funding. Your competitors are well-funded. The panel has three tough investors who've seen hundreds of agritech pitches.
scenarios.pitch_topic: KrishiSense — affordable IoT sensor kits for Indian smallholder farmers

predefined_metrics.revenue: ₹8 lakh/month from sensor sales + ₹2 lakh from data subscriptions
predefined_metrics.ask: ₹50 lakh competition prize + ₹1 crore matching investment for 15% equity

coaching_tips: Hardware is hard — acknowledge the challenges upfront
Show your unit economics clearly (₹3K cost, margins, replacement cycle)
Explain how you handle farmer adoption (trust, simplicity, local language)
Address the competitive threat from government schemes and larger players
learning_objectives: Present a hardware + software business model
Handle skepticism about agritech adoption challenges
Defend against competitive and regulatory concerns

storybook_pages.title: The Farmer's Gamble
storybook_pages.text: Ramu Kaka has 2 acres of cotton in Warangal. Every season is a gamble — too much water, too little, pests he can't see until it's too late. Last year, he lost 40% of his crop. He couldn't afford his daughter's school fees. Millions of Indian farmers share his story.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian farmer looking worried at a struggling cotton crop field in Telangana, dry cracked soil, wilting plants, Indian rural farming landscape, emotional and gritty, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: KrishiSense Changes the Game
storybook_pages.text: Your sensor kit costs ₹3,000 — affordable for a small farmer. Stick it in the soil, connect to the app (works in Hindi), and get real-time alerts: 'Irrigation needed in 6 hours.' 'Disease pattern detected — spray neem solution.' 800 farmers already swear by it. Yields are up 22%.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Close-up of a small IoT sensor device planted in Indian farmland with a smartphone showing a Hindi app with crop health data, green healthy crops around the sensor, technology meets agriculture, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Final Round
storybook_pages.text: Hyderabad's HICC convention center. The national startup competition finals. Five startups. ₹50 lakh on the line. Three investors who've funded and buried agritech startups. The previous pitcher had slick slides but no traction. You have 800 real farmers. Let's go.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Grand Hyderabad convention center stage with national startup competition setup, judges panel, large screen showing startup logos, young Indian founder walking to the stage confidently, competition atmosphere, illustration style

transfer_exercises.game_context: Managing resources across multiple rounds to reach the best outcome
transfer_exercises.real_world: Planning study time over a semester rather than cramming before exams
transfer_exercises.challenge: Create a resource management plan for your next month: budget time/money/energy across competing priorities.

transfer_exercises.game_context: Recovering from negative events across game rounds
transfer_exercises.real_world: Maintaining performance after setbacks in a sports season or project
transfer_exercises.challenge: Track your energy/mood for 5 days. Notice patterns. What depletes you? What restores you?

glossary_terms.definition: The process of selecting among alternatives based on available information and values.
glossary_terms.example: Choosing between two career paths based on income, passion, and long-term growth.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Good decision-making combines rational analysis with awareness of cognitive biases that distort judgment.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Leaders make high-stakes decisions daily — the quality of their process matters as much as the decision itself.

glossary_terms.definition: Analyzing information objectively to form a well-reasoned judgment.
glossary_terms.example: Questioning whether a statistic is representative before using it to make a decision.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Critical thinking involves identifying assumptions, evaluating evidence, and considering alternative perspectives.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Journalists fact-check before publishing; scientists replicate experiments before claiming discoveries.

glossary_terms.definition: The belief that abilities can be developed through effort and learning from failure.
glossary_terms.example: Seeing a poor game result as feedback on what to practice, not evidence of being bad at the game.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Research by Carol Dweck shows people with growth mindsets achieve more and recover better from setbacks.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Students who believe intelligence is fixed give up when challenged; those with growth mindset persist and improve.

title: Investor Pitch
description: Pitch your startup idea to a panel of tough, realistic investors. Refine your narrative, handle hard questions, and learn what separates a compelling pitch from a forgettable one.
coaching_moment: Pitch your startup idea to a panel of tough, realistic investors. Refine your narrative, handle hard questions, and learn what separates a compelling pitch from a forgettable one.
cultural_context: India's booming venture capital ecosystem — with investors active in every sector from fintech to agritech — means more Indian founders are pitching investors than ever before. The ability to communicate vision, data, and conviction clearly is a foundational entrepreneurial skill.
learning_objectives: Develop critical thinking through negotiation gameplay
Build self-awareness about your strengths and areas for growth
reflection_prompt: Where did you give ground, and where did you hold it? What did the other side teach you about your own priorities?
